topics.title: Introduction to Magnets and Their Types
topics.summary: Magnets, first discovered as natural lodestones and later produced artificially, are used for various purposes including navigation and everyday items, and come in different shapes.
learning_objectives: Understand the historical significance of magnets in navigation.
Identify naturally occurring magnets (lodestones) and artificial magnets.
Recognize common shapes of artificial magnets.
Appreciate the presence of magnets in daily life.

subtopics.title: The Discovery and Everyday Use of Magnets
subtopics.summary: The chapter begins with a story illustrating the historical need for navigation tools, leading to the discovery of magnets and their use in devices like the magnetic compass, as well as their presence in common household items.
subtopics.content: Reshma lives in a coastal town of Kerala and is very fond of writing short stories. Her grandmother loves listening to her stories, so Reshma was writing a new story to share with her grandmother on her 60th birthday. Exploring Magnets The story was based on a ship carrying spices from Kerala for trade in the olden days. Reshma was aware that in those days, the sailors used stars to find directions at night. But in her story, a situation arose wherein the sailors got caught in a storm with an overcast sky and stars were not visible. Reshma could not take her story forward as she could not think of a way for sailors to find directions. She searched for in formation on the in ternet and her school library. She learnt that the travellers used a device, known as a magnetic compass, for finding directions. Reshma had seen pencil boxes and purses which had magnets to keep them closed. A writing board in her school also had a duster with a magnet. But she had never looked at those carefully. She now became curious to learn more about magnets and magnetic compasses. Reprint 2026-27
learning_objectives: Recognize the historical importance of magnets in navigation.
Identify everyday objects that utilize magnets.
Develop curiosity about magnetic properties.

subtopics.title: Natural and Artificial Magnets and Their Shapes
subtopics.summary: This subtopic distinguishes between naturally occurring lodestones and modern artificial magnets, illustrating how magnets are made from iron and come in various shapes like bar, U-shaped, and ring magnets.
subtopics.content: The magnets used by sailors in the olden days were based on naturally occurring magnets, known as lodestones which were discovered in ancient times. Later on, people found out that magnets could also be made from pieces of iron. Nowadays, we have magnets made of different materials. The magnets that you find in your school laboratory and those used in pencil boxes, stickers, toys are all artificial magnets (Fig. 4.1). The magnets can be of various shapes, some of which are shown in Fig. 4.2. Fig. 4.1: Some common items that have magnets attached to them 4.1 Magnetic and Non-magnetic Materials Bar magnet U-shaped magnet Ring magnet Fig. 4.2: Magnets of different shapes Curiosity | Textbook of Science | Grade 6 Reprint 2026-27
learning_objectives: Differentiate between natural magnets (lodestones) and artificial magnets.
Identify various common shapes of artificial magnets.
Understand that magnets can be made from iron and other materials.

topics.title: Magnetic and Non-magnetic Materials
topics.summary: This topic defines magnetic materials as those attracted by a magnet, such as iron, nickel, and cobalt, and non-magnetic materials as those not attracted by a magnet. An activity helps students identify these materials.
learning_objectives: Define magnetic materials.
Define non-magnetic materials.
Identify examples of magnetic and non-magnetic materials.
Conduct an experiment to classify materials as magnetic or non-magnetic.

topics.title: Poles of a Magnet
topics.summary: This topic explains that a magnet's attractive force is strongest at its ends, called poles (North and South), and emphasizes that these poles always exist in pairs, even if the magnet is broken.
learning_objectives: Locate the poles of a magnet.
Understand that magnetic attraction is strongest at the poles.
Explain why a magnet cannot have a single pole.

subtopics.title: Observing Magnetic Attraction (Activity 4.2)
subtopics.summary: An activity with iron filings demonstrates that magnetic attraction is concentrated at the ends of a magnet, defining these areas as the North and South poles.

Reprint 2026-27 If we have noticed the direction where the Sun rises or sets, we have an approximate idea of where East or West is. Hence, we can locate the direction along which the magnet rests.
These ends of the magnet are called the two poles of the magnet—the North pole and the South pole. Most of the iron filings stick to the poles of a magnet of any shape.
It is not possible to obtain a magnet with a single pole. If a magnet is broken into smaller pieces, North and South poles always exist in pairs even in the smallest piece of the magnet.
A single North pole or a South pole cannot exist.
learning_objectives: Observe the distribution of magnetic force around a magnet using iron filings.
Define the North and South poles of a magnet.
State the principle that poles always exist in pairs.

topics.title: Finding Directions
topics.summary: This topic explains how a freely suspended magnet always aligns itself in the North-South direction, a property used in magnetic compasses to find directions, and that Earth itself acts as a giant magnet.
learning_objectives: Describe the behavior of a freely suspended magnet.
Explain how a magnetic compass works.
Identify the North-seeking and South-seeking poles of a magnet.
Understand that Earth behaves as a giant magnet.

subtopics.title: Freely Suspended Magnets and Direction (Activity 4.3)
subtopics.summary: An experiment demonstrates that a freely suspended bar magnet always comes to rest in the North-South direction, distinguishing its North and South poles.

Reprint 2026-27 A freely suspended magnet comes to rest along the north-south direction. The end of the magnet that points to wards north direction is called the North-seeking pole or the North pole of the magnet. The other end that points to wards the South direction is called the South-seeking pole or the South
pole of the magnet. A freely suspended magnet rests along the north-south direction because our
Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet.
Repeat this activity with a small iron bar in place of the bar magnet. What do you observe? Does it always rest along north-south direction? It does not. It can rest along any direction. This implies that only magnets rest along north-south direction. This activity provides us with a way to test whether a piece of metal is a magnet or not.
learning_objectives: Perform an experiment to observe the directional property of a magnet.
Identify the North and South poles of a freely suspended magnet.
Differentiate a magnet from a non-magnetic material using its directional property.

subtopics.title: The Magnetic Compass
subtopics.summary: The magnetic compass, a device with a freely rotating magnetic needle, uses the directional property of magnets to indicate the North-South direction for navigation.
subtopics.content:
The property of a freely suspended magnet to always rest along the north-south direction is used to find directions.
Based on this, a small device called a magnetic compass was developed in olden days for finding directions. It has a magnet in the shape of a needle which can rotate freely (Fig. 4.6). The needle of a magnetic compass in dicates the north-south direction.
The compass is kept at the place where we wish to know the directions. After some time, the needle comes to rest in the north-south direction.
The compass box is then gently rotated until the north and south marked on the dial are aligned with the needle. Now all directions at that place are as in dicated on the dial.
A magnetic compass is usually a small circular box with a transparent cover on it, as shown in Fig. 4.6.
The magnet, in the shape of a needle, is mounted on a pin standing on the bottom of the box. This needle is balanced on the pin in such a manner that it can move around this point easily, that is, it can rotate freely. The end of the needle which rests in the North direction is usually painted red. Below the needle, there is a dial with directions marked on it.
How can we make our own magnetic compass?

subtopics.title: Making Your Own Magnetic Compass (Activity 4.4)
subtopics.summary: This subtopic provides instructions for magnetizing an iron needle and constructing a simple magnetic compass using a cork and water, similar to ancient navigation tools.
subtopics.content:
Activity 4.4: Let us construct

‹
‹
Collect a few materials like a cork piece, iron sewing needle, a permanent bar magnet, a glass bowl, and water.

‹

Place the iron sewing needle on a wooden table. Then keep any one pole of the magnet at one end of the needle. Move the magnet over the needle along its length as shown in Fig.
4.7a. When it reaches the other end of the needle, lift it up.

‹
‹
Bring the same pole of the magnet you started with to the same end of the sewing needle from which you began, and repeat the previous step. Repeat this process at least 30 to 40 times.

‹

Bring some iron filings or steel pins near the needle.
If the pins or iron filings get attracted to the needle, then that means that the needle has become a magnet.

‹

Pass this needle through the cork horizontally.
Float the cork in a glass bowl filled with water, such that the needle always remains above the level of water as shown in Fig. 4.7b.

‹

When the needle comes to rest, your magnetic compass is ready for use. Note the direction in which either side of the needle points.

‹

Rotate the cork gently and wait till it stops rotating.
Repeat this a few more times. Do the ends of the needle always point in the same direction?

topics.title: Attraction and Repulsion between Magnets
topics.summary: This topic explains the fundamental principle of magnetism: like poles repel each other, and unlike poles attract each other. It also describes how magnets attract non-magnetic materials like iron and that magnetic effects can act through non-magnetic substances.
learning_objectives: State the law of magnetic attraction and repulsion.
Distinguish between attraction and repulsion.
Explain how a magnet can be identified by its property of repulsion.
Describe how magnetic effects can pass through non-magnetic materials.

topics.title: Fun with Magnets
topics.summary: This topic presents several engaging activities and thought experiments to explore the practical and intriguing applications of magnets, demonstrating their ability to interact with objects without direct contact.
learning_objectives: Develop creative uses for magnets in daily life.
Understand that magnets can exert force without direct contact.
Apply knowledge of attraction and repulsion in fun scenarios.

topics.title: Magnet Care and Storage
topics.summary: This section provides crucial advice on how to properly handle and store magnets to prevent demagnetization and ensure their longevity, emphasizing that magnets should not be heated, dropped, or kept near electronic devices.
learning_objectives: Identify actions that can damage or demagnetize magnets.
Explain proper storage techniques for magnets to maintain their strength.
Understand the importance of keeping magnets away from electronic devices.

subtopics.title: Handling and Storing Magnets
subtopics.summary: Learn how to properly care for magnets by avoiding heat, drops, or impacts, and how to store them with unlike poles facing each other, separated by wood, and with soft iron pieces across their ends to maintain their magnetic strength.
